I had some trouble loading a program into my Blue Ram yesterday... let me give you some background:

I ran a short 17-byte program yesterday in the $6000 area of my Blue Ram via AstroBASIC.  I actually typed the program in myself (imagine that!).  The program is from page 7 of the "Z-80 Minicourse," here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/astrocade_z80_mini-course.pdf

The program, which I refer to as "Colors" (but is unnamed in the book), POKEs decimal numbers into any area that you wish (since the program is relocatable).  The book presumes the user has no expanded memory and the program originally resides at $4EFC (or 20220 decimal).  On real hardware I had no trouble at all POKEing the program to $6000 (or 24576 in decimal).  I also had no trouble running the program by calling it with CALL 24576.  The program, although short, is quite colorful and was worth the
effort.  It's one of those popular Rainbow Effect displays where the
user uses Hand Controller 1 to get a stable pattern on the screen.

I converted the program from decimal to hex, and then quickly disassembled it.  Here is the program's listing after being assembled using the ZMAC assembler:

   1:            ; "Colors"
   2:            ; From Z-80 Minicourse
   3:           
   4:    6000                      ORG $6000
   5:                          
   6:    6000  3C                  INC     A
   7:    6001  D304                OUT     ($04),A
   8:    6003  20FB                JR      NZ,$6000
   9:    6005  DB1C                IN      A,(1CH)
  10:    6007  47                  LD      B,A
  11:    6008  DB15                IN      A,(15H)
  12:    600A  10FC                DJNZ    $6008
  13:    600C  FE01                CP      01H
  14:    600E  20F0                JR      NZ,$6000
  15:    6010  C9                  RET    
  16:           
**** Colors.z80 ****

Statistics:

     0    symbols
    17    bytes


I took the 17-byte binary file and converted it to a BML file using BIN2BML (I've been using that program EVERY SINGLE DAY for quite a while now!).  Then I converted the BML file to a WAV program via AstroWAV.  From there, I loaded it via AstroBASIC into the Blue Ram using this command:

:INPUT %(24576)

I've been using this technique lately to load cartridge images without trouble.  However, the load ended with a question mark.  Knowing that meant a bad load, I didn't expect the program to work.  Well, despite the obvious load error I decided to try running the program anyway.  I ran it with:

CALL 24576

Well, what so you know.  The program ran fine.  Can anyone think of why I might have gotten a load error?  Do you think it has something to do with BIN2BML, AstroWAV, or AstroBASIC?  Lance or Paul, do you think you could assemble the above program and see if you can get it to load without a load error via either your Viper or Lil' White RAM expansions?

10009:
I was trying to think of every potentially relevant difference, but as has become apparent, the actually important one was what cart we were using.  And the problem, perhaps not surprisingly, again comes down to the light pen interrupts.  I'm sure this crept in as soon as the code switched over to the MAME implementation, though it wouldn't have been apparent until I kept it from crashing.  The old Astrocade MESS code actually didn't account for the light pen interrupts at all, though perhaps this was preferable to the current, apparently incorrect, implementation.

As far as the anonymous timers are concerned, I'm vaguely familiar with that term.  I think that they're using deprecated functions to track the interrupts, and these don't work with the save state system.  I'm not sure, at the moment, what the correct way to do this is.

As for the other questions that came up--

Using the command line version can be nice for development, for instance if you want to print debugging information to the command line.  For regular users, MESSUI should be fine.  In fact, that's often what I use.

I'm not sure why you'd have trouble with drivers other than astrocdw.  You can check the code for the BIOS information:

ROM_START( astrocde )
	ROM_REGION( 0x10000, "maincpu", 0 )
	ROM_LOAD( "astro.bin",  0x0000, 0x2000, CRC(ebc77f3a) SHA1(b902c941997c9d150a560435bf517c6a28137ecc) )
	ROM_CART_LOAD( "cart", 0x2000, 0x8000, 0 )
ROM_END

ROM_START( astrocdl )
	ROM_REGION( 0x10000, "maincpu", 0 )
	ROM_LOAD( "ballyhlc.bin",  0x0000, 0x2000, CRC(d7c517ba) SHA1(6b2bef5d970e54ed204549f58ba6d197a8bfd3cc) )
	ROM_CART_LOAD( "cart", 0x2000, 0x8000, 0 )
ROM_END

ROM_START( astrocdw )
	ROM_REGION( 0x10000, "maincpu", 0 )
	ROM_LOAD( "bioswhit.bin",  0x0000, 0x2000, CRC(6eb53e79) SHA1(d84341feec1a0a0e8aa6151b649bc3cf6ef69fbf) )
	ROM_CART_LOAD( "cart", 0x2000, 0x8000, 0 )
ROM_END

So the astrocde driver (the most common BIOS), is expecting a file named "astro.bin".  You can keep this in MESS's "roms" folder in a ZIP file named "astrocde.zip".

Paul

Ward Shrake and I used to talk about this.  He used to archive Vic-20 cartridges way back in the dark ages of the Internet (the early to mid-1990's).  He took offense (with very good reason, I think) when someone told him that what he did didn't matter at all.  If he didn't do archive it, then SOMEONE else would do it.  He thinks people like this believe in Internet Elves (tm).  It's as though these people believe that no one is REALLY doing the work and that it just happens by magic.  There is really NO magic behind the scenes.  There is just a lot of dedication.

To me, it quite unbelievable the amount of effort that has gone into giant projects such as Linux.  Hell, it's an insult to call Linux a "project."  It's a damn operating system!  Another good example of a huge project is MAME, and it's offshoot, MESS.  The work that goes on that gets all of these arcade systems emulated is incredible.

It's not just the WORK, but the WORKING TOGETHER that really amazes me.  That's why I respect this Bally Alley discussion group so much.  Without the help of all the people that contribute, the BallyAlley.com site would only be a shadow of what it currently is now.  Thanks to everybody who contributes!  Also thanks to those that just have questions or wanna BS about the "old days."  You make this hobby interesting!

Michael Garber has a helpful program called "Color Pick" in the homebrew area of BallyAlley.com, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_homebrew/ml_homebrew.html

The program works on real hardware, but not on newer versions of MESS.  This is already known.  In order to use the program, which is quite helpful, you have to assemble it.  This is where the error is:

        DO     (SETOUT)   ; Set Display Ports
        DB     (VERTLN*2) ; Vertical Blanking Line (90 lines)
        DB     44         ; Left/Right Color Boundary
        DB     $18        ; Interrupt Mode                    <--- ERROR HERE

This is the same error that was plaguing "Crazy Climber," and I presume "War" as well.  The interrupt mode is setup incorrectly.  Thanks to Richard Degler for figuring this out a short while back and providing the fix via private email exchanges.  To make "Color Pick" work, make this change:

        DB     $08        ; Interrupt Mode

After you assemble the program with this fix, it will run fine in all versions of MESS.

I used "Color Pick" today to help identify some colors in the "Songs" cartridge.  The program works like a charm!  Thanks, Michael, for providing this useful program!  Without it, I'd have NO idea what these colors are in "Songs:"

; ($217D) - Color List [for "Songs"]
COLTAB  DB     $04          ; Color 3 Left (Gray)
        DB     $0A          ; Color 2 Left (Purplish-Blue)
        DB     $07          ; Color 1 Left (White)
        DB     $63          ; Color 0 Left (Brownish-Orange)
        DB     $10          ; Color 3 Right (Blue)
        DB     $44          ; Color 2 Right (Pink)
        DB     $55          ; Color 1 Right (Orange)
        DB     $22          ; Color 0 Right (Purple)

It's too bad that my color vocabulary is terrible.  In the comments for the Color Table (above), I'm describing color $63 as "Brownish-Orange."  There is undoubtedly a more precise term than that!  If only my parents had bought me a bigger box of Crayola crayons that had more than eight colors, then I wouldn't have this problem.  ...Okay, I admit it.  I had a box of sixty-four crayons and it still didn't help me!

In reference to what was mentioned yesterday about reading "tech" postings, I have these questions:

1) Who made it this far-- who read the entire post and not just skimmed it?

2) Who UNDERSTANDS it, at least in theory?

3) Who could make the fix to the source code, assemble it, and have a "cartridge" that would work with all versions of MESS?

Adam

P.S.  I suppose I should probably fix the version of "Color Pick" that is currently online so that people don't have to read this post to know about this fix.  For now, in case you want to check, I'll just leave it be...

Colors in MESS are an approximation of the colors produced by an
actual Bally / Astrocade and its resistor-ladder hardware set-up.

Using "ColorPicker.bin" under MESS requires adjusting the Z/X key
(substitute knob) sensitivity so it doesn't take a full minute to
go from 0 to 255, but not so mutch that you can't reach 0 or 255.


I'll assume Adam is adding to my dis-assembly of Scot Norris's :

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/songs_[2008_02_28].asm

where I left all the LABELs as "L2xxx" since they refered to set
locations in the prototype EPROM.  Please use the NOTE Names from
"HVGLIB.H" - since I always meant to go back and do that one day.


Anyway, my comments had called the colors in the un-nammed table :

L217D:____;_Color_Table
________DB______$04,$0A,$07,$63__;_Grey,_Blue,_White,_Orange
________DB______$10,$44,$55,$22__;_Dark_Blue,_Pink,_Peach,_Purple

with '_' for spaces, since I can't get Yahoo! to not eat them.
Also had some TABs in there which would have made it more ragged.


Yes, I read all of all the messages, no matter how poorly quoted.
Speaking of Mike White, he probably originated "$18" originally,
(misspelled as "origional") in his Basic-Carts and example code.

Richard Degler

In the auction Michael said that he doesn't know how many of these cartridges were made.  Well, only 32 were made!  So, calling this rare is an extreme understatement.  Here is the information from the Bally Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ:


Music Maker
     Astrocade Inc.                            #4003  8K cart  1985.
AKA Music Maker 1, Music Composer.  Started by Bally before 1979 as two cartridges but never released. When Astrocade came on, development went into a 2000 baud tape interface.  A prototype was sent to George Moses with a keypad overlay and instructions.  In 1985 Leroy Flamm engineered circuit boards that supported the tape interface.  This cartridge never saw an official release.  Only 32 working units (with the built-in interface) were made.  Mike White retyped the instructions that appeared (Arcadian vol.7 pg.95-102).  Very few were then sold by Mike White or ABC Hobbycraft.  Written by Scot L. Norris. (References: Cursor pg.73, Arcadian vol.1 pg.23, vol.3 pg 31,41,66,91,121, vol.4 pg.33,75,84, vol.5 pg 16,36,46,66, vol.6 pg.1,99, and vol.7 pg.2,13,46,67,94-102, Michigan Astrobugs Newsletter Jul.82 pg.1)


I own this cartridge, and it's neat.  I have never really given it the time that it deserves to learn how to use it.  There is great potential here, I'll tell you that.  If this cartridge had really been among the original releases for the Bally Arcade (as it was supposed to have been), then I imagine that it would have been used by schools.  I mean it.  Over the last couple of days, I've been playing around with the music subtroutines in the "Music processor" in the Bally ROM and this cartridge has access to those and makes it EASY and VISUAL to use them.  Many people have commented on the Bally's quality sound.  This cartridge allows a laymen to play around with that!

I've always wanted to have a section of downloadable songs for the "Music Maker" cartridge, but I've never been able to get mine to save and then reload.  The save function obviously DOES work, at least so much as that it gives a header, tones, and then an end tone.  Reloading is the problem for me.  I've tried running saved "Music Maker" files through Ballybin, but it never cleans them up properly (If I recall, I get an error-- but then, Ballybin is meant to work with AstroBASIC files!).  Paul Thacker mentioned recently something (using a "Raw" command-line switch, I think) that I might try with Ballybin to make it work, but I've not tried it yet.  "Music Maker's" tape interface is BASED on AstroBASIC's interface.  As everybody knows, the AstroBASIC tape interface can be temperamental, but once you figure it out, it adds an entire dimension to using the Bally/Astrocade.  I'm sure that the same is true with "Music Maker."

If you're interested in collecting, then I suggest HEAVILY that you pick this cart up while you can!  If you like playing games, and investigating how carts work, then also give this title a try-- there is a LOT here.  I'd absolutely LOVE to work with someone else that has this cartridge.  I'm sure that a couple of people together could figure it out and have some fun with it... and add a nice new section to BallyAlley.com!

Think about getting it.  If this were a perfect world, there should be a bidding war over this cartridge!

might have slipped me a twenty under the table to praise this
cartridge.  I assure you that this is not the case.  It is just that
this is one of the most unappreciated cartridges in the
Bally/Astrocade's library.  This auction and posting just happens to have provided me with a
 platform to speak the truth about it.

Unlike "War," which only had twenty copies released, "Crazy Climber" is going to have more than twenty copies made.  We're not sure how many yet but certainly not in the numbers that you'd see for an Atari 2600 release.  Still, through Ken Lill, we have the means to make as many PCBs as we want-- though now it's the cartridge shell that are the limiting factor.  I wouldn't worry about missing out on it if you're leaving in March though.  The plan is to make an announcement for the game soon... we're just waiting on, basically two things:

1)  Mike is going to play the game on real hardware.  Currently, he only uses it on MESS and has still never seen the game running on an Astrocade (though I have-- it works fine).  Michael now has an EPROM version of the cart, so this should happen soon.  If he likes what he sees and all goes okay then we can proceed to step two.

2)  After Michael approves the cart on real hardware then "Crazy Climber" will be sent to two members of this forum (one via an EPROM cart and the other as a cart image).  We'll get some of feedback from both of them.  Michael isn't looking to make significant changes to the game.  This is a step to eliminate any possible bugs that may have somehow slipped through without he or I noticing.

After Michael tests the cart and the two other people play the game and give feedback, then I'll make an announcement.  Hopefully this all happens before March, but if it slips into March then it shouldn't be TOO far into Match.  Now, the first announcement is going to be just to raise enough funds to get the PCBs done.  This is going to cost about $750 or so.  So, at first, the announcement will only accept twenty orders and these people will have to wait about 6-8 weeks for shipment of the game.  These will have to be the patient folks.  After the PCBs arrive, then more copies will be available (we figure 40-50 games total).

So, now everybody knows where we stand with the release of "Crazy Climber."

Adam

10054:
I just finished following "How to Use the Blue Ram BASIC 'Play%( )' Command, A Tutorial," by George Moses from the Arcadian newsletter (June 17, 1983, Vol. 5, no. 8, pg. 128). This really was the reason that I setup a spare USB keyboard to act like a Bally keypad. I'm one of the few people who can actually use Blue Ram BASIC on a real console, as I do have a RAM expansion. Most people, of course, DON'T have this ability, but I was curious how well the beta version of MESS that supports RAM expansion would work. I used MESS 0.141u1 (Feb. 4, 2011). This is the recent build that Paul Thacker contributed to. Note that 

I'm glad to say that everything worked very well! I ran into no difficulty whatsoever using my keypad and my new MESS keyboard mapping. First I used the PLAY command to play a few sounds and very brief music that is stored in the on-board ROM ("Taps," "Funeral March," and "Gunshot Sound"). After that went well, I typed in the BASIC program to enter data starting at $607F (which is in the newly created RAM expansion area of MESS-- so this is a good test). I then input 56 bytes using the short BASIC program included in the tutorial. The data is used by the Music Processor (an On-Board ROM Routine) to play some music. The tutorial doesn't say what the music actually is. After I typed it up and played it, I discovered that the data is the music for the beginning of "Chopsticks."

I used "Save State" to save what I typed-up and I've attached the file. It is called, "Blue Ram BASIC (Arcadian, Play Command, Vol 5, No 8, Page 128).sta" This Save State will ONLY work with the version of MESS that supports the extended RAM area. This version of MESS does not yet have a public release, so you'll have to do some digging if you want to try it out (follow Paul's links on how to get this version of MESS up and running-- it was EASY). I'm including this Save State in case Paul (or anyone) wants to use it for testing purposes. After the Save State is loaded you can list the BASIC program that was used to input the machine language data or play the music using this command: PLAY%(!607F).

I do have a question: how do I PRINT one byte at a time, in hex (if possible). For instance, if I want to step through the data that I just input at $607F, how could I check it?

It's nice that I can use Save State (although you can't count on it for use between versions)... but I sure wish that MESS could save in a file format that could be loaded onto a REAL Astrocade via AstroBASIC using Ballybin and AstroWAV. Maybe now that this extra RAM is available in MESS (well, not QUITE yet, but soon I guess), some people will be more willing to try to update the emulator.

Adam
10055:
while in BRB 1.1, set the NB (number base) to 16 (hex) and do a loop. for A = 0
to n Step 2;Print %(a)" ";NEXT A
That will separate the bytes with a space so that it is easier to see them.
Ken
P.S. remember to set the NB back to 10 so you can tell the line lumbers in
decimal.

10056:
In BRB1.1 ("PL." worked in 1.0 also) mask off the low byte with :

NB=16
FOR A=!607F to A+55PRINT A," = ",%(A)^!FF;NEXT A
NB=10

where ^ is the 'UP ARROW' key (and print HEX Numbers is optional.)
Don't think the Arrow OPs, OP, PLAY or RPL worked in Viper or HRB.


What was supposed to come after "Note that" below ?

Just putting my 2 cents in here. The S-Video unit uses the same LM1889 Video
processing chip. IT is what does the summing to come up with the colors. The
Bally main unit comes up with 4 signals to make all of it's colors. They are R-Y
(Red minus Video), B-Y (Blue minus Video) and Chroma and Video. The 2 colors R-Y
and B-Y are combined to create the G-Y signal. THEN the Video is added to create
the Red, Blue and Green colors used to make the color palette. The Chroma is the
"contrast" part of the equation. It could almost be called the brightness, but
not quite. Hard to depict the differences here, and it may be too technical for
most people.
      So to say that the resistive ladder is in the custom chip is really not
accurate. It is in the modulator.
Ken

I've seen programs use simple tricks for getting this functionality.  I don't remember what program it was--probably one of the 300 baud ones I processed over the last few months--but it was something like:

IF (A+B) do something
IF (AxB) do something

Assume A and B are 1 if a certain condition is true, and 0 if it's false.
In the first case, the statement will be true if A OR B are true.
In the second case, the statement will only be true if A AND B are true.

These can also be combined in more complicated ways:

IF ((A+B)x(C+D)) means IF ((A OR B) AND (C OR D))

Does this cover what you're wanting to do?

if you insert numbers into the equations, they will prove not to be accurate as
an OR

IF (-1+1) do something  would end up with a zero and it would not do anything
even though there was a number in both variables.
The AND would not be a true AND in the sense of ANDing. ANDing binararily will
add the two together.
The second IF statement is only good to use if you expect that one on the 2
variables might contain a zero. Then, and only then, the statement would give
you a zero out. ALL other circumstances would give you a 1 out.
Ken

No, but it is useful information to keep in mind.

As Richard presumed, I would like to use the AND operator to mask a certain byte.  In my case, I want to mask Ports 21 and 22.  Both of these ports control volume, like this:

Voice A, Volume (Port 22, Four LSB)
Voice B, Volume (Port 22, Four MSB)
Voice C, Volume (Port 21, Four LSB)
Noise, Enable (Port 21, Bit 6)

(Just in case you're not aware, LSB means Lowest Significant Bits and MSB means Most Significant Bits-- so that's half a byte each, or a nibble.)

I don't have to set the initial volume using a mask, but if I want to change just ONE volume later on, then I DO have to use a mask.  Full volume is 15 (from 0-15, or sixteen different volumes).  In Bally BASIC (or AstroBASIC using NT=-1) I could set the initial volume of Voice A and B to about half of full volume, seven, like this:

&(22)=119

I skipped an intermediate step.  First I had to figure-out in Hexadecimal what would set the LSB and MSB to seven.  That hex number is: $77 (that makes sense, right?).  The number 119 is decimal for $77.  Great.  Now we've set the volume of voices A and B to about halfway of full volume.  Let's presume that Voices A and B have already been set to some frequency (we won't concern ourselves with Voice C).  Now we can hear whatever sounds that Voices A and B are playing.  If we want to change Voice B to volume 4 and leave Voice A at volume 7, then that's easy.  Set Port 22 to $47 like this:

&(22)=71

Now we've changed the volume.  As you can see, since BASIC uses decimal numbers instead of hex, it sort of disguises what you're doing.  That's why it's nice that Blue Ram BASIC allows entering hex numbers by putting an exclamation mark in front of them, like this:

@(22)=!47

Nice, right?  So what's the trouble, then?  I have the ability to set the volume of both Voices.  Well, what if I want to change the volume of Voice B and not change the volume of Voice A... but I don't know the current volume of Voice A?  Easy.  I use the AND operator... which I've now learned AstroBASIC doesn't have.  With a mask, I usually think in binary, although to mask a full nibble (four bits) thinking in binary isn't really necessary because you will always use $F.  But, to explain, I am going to speak in binary.  If you feel like you're confused in a few seconds just smile and nod.  Let's say Port 22's byte holds (as above) $77.  In binary, this is represented as:

0111 0111  - I have separated each nibble by a space to make it easier to read.

If we want to only change Voice B (MSB) and NOT Voice A (LSB), then we want to "mask off" the lower four bits.  If we want to change Voice B to four and keep Voice A at it's current volume (pretend that you don't know that it is currently set at seven), then you would AND them together and then add the the Volume, in hex, that you want for Voice B (MSB) to the result of the AND operation.  It will work like this (some details about how AND works follow this process):

0111 0111 - Current Value in Port 22
0000 1111 - AND Mask (Discard MSB, Keep LSB)
---------
0000 0111 - New Intermediate Value

Notice that the intermediate value of Voice A has not been changed, but that Voice B is now zero.  Now I add the value that I want for Voice B (which is $40):

0000 0111 - Intermediate Value (Voice A is still $7)
0100 0000 - Add Bits we want to change (Voice B's new Value of $4)
---------
0100 0111 - Final Value in Port 22

Port 22's value is now $47.  We changed the volume of only one of the ports while having absolutely NO effect on the other port.

If you don't know how the AND operator works, then this is probably confusing the hell out of you and you're scratching your head now asking yourself something like, "That doesn't make any sense, Adam.  Let's talk about games.  Come on, can't we talk about 'Galactic Invasion' or 'The Incredible Wizard?' or, hey, when is 'Crazy Climber' getting release?"  Sorry, it's too late for that now-- ya got me talk'en.

A quick refresher in how AND works (if you're still awake at this point, then this will surely put you to sleep):

0 AND 0 = 0
0 AND 1 = 0
1 AND 0 = 0
1 AND 1 = 1

So, in essence a MASK of four one's for the LSB (Voice A) will leave the LSB UNCHANGED and the MASK of all zero's for the MSB's leaves VOICE B at zero.  This is the key to using AND.  You can mask off whichever parts of a byte you want to use or not use.  If you only want to deal with one bit at a time (which is rather common, actually), then you can do that without changing the contents of the entire byte.

Something that isn't obvious from above is that we only changed Port 22 in the final step.  We keep the intermediate step of the mask's result in a variable and THEN we add it to Port 22's value, which is what finally changes the volume level of Voice B.

Now, what is good about AstroBASIC is that Jay Fenton updated it so that it is far and away easier to deal with the Sound Ports.  Indeed, NONE of the above would need to be done anymore because Jay likes BASIC programmers.  He added variables for the Sound Ports.  So, to change the volume of Voice B (variable VB) to 4 and not affect anything else it's simple:

VB=4

Well, thanks, Jay.  I'm sure there are thousands of BASIC programmers who love you for that!

So, you're probably asking yourself why I'm torturing myself using the Sound Ports directly if Jay went through all the trouble to add Sound Variables to AstroBASIC.  Well, the answer is simple.  I'm really learning about the Sound Ports to get a handle on them in machine language... which has no such variables (of course).  But, again, the System ROM does have music and sound routines that make the task MUCH easier.  Still, knowing how the ports work is still necessary.  Since it seems that Blue Ram BASIC does have the AND operator, I'll just use that version of BASIC for my tinkering around with the Sound Ports.

For C programmers or assembly programmers this is really old news and this was probably a refresher.  If you dabble in electronics, but don't program, then you already know how AND works as it's a simple component used ALL the time.  For everyone else, the above information is probably a little confusing-- although I did my best to present it simply.  The trouble is, to get understand this information, you already need some background.  So, if you didn't understand this, then keep this posting in mind and maybe in the future you can come back to it and say to yourself, "Wow, NOW it all makes sense to me!"

1) Atlantis is AB only.  Besides saving the title screen to tape,
which BB does not do, it uses noise variables NM and NV effects.
Looks like he typed his name in mixed-case in the original byline.


2) Gravity (vol.6 issue 5 not 6) AB only since it uses *(array),
and you could simply use this loader on the command line (NLN):
> for A=0to 14;input *(A);next A          [No Line Number ^^^]


3) Sink the U-Boat ("You sunk my BATTLESHIP!" ?) issue ??, anyway
both AB and BB have the same size 104 character Line Input Buffer
and some BASIC programs stuff machine code up in there when ran.
AB de-interlaces each text line into this buffer before executing
which would overwrite that code when program lines were too long.

If you wanted to do MAZE AVENGER from vol. 6 issue 11-12 Page 100
> for A=20237to A+40step 2;input %(A);next A   LIB starts at 20154
so each line needs to be less than 83 characters long (running AB)
But wait, that fills up to 20278 and the Buffer ends at 20258, eh?
There's 72 bytes for overflow below the system Stack, so it's OK.


4) Video:Video watch 4-color graphics on a split screen, AB or BB

Notice R&L's update to 4D2 (now AB only) on Pg. 126 has the loader
built in, and will only prompt you for it if the array is empty.


But has OUTPOST 19 for Extended Basic on Page 118 been archived?


Richard

10150:
When I archive a program from tape, the first thing I do is to play the tape into my sound card and record it in an audio editing program, Audacity.  I then save this as a .wav file.  .wav is an uncompressed audio file format used, for example, on CDs.  Since this hasn't been processed in any way to improve the quality, we call this a raw recording.

There are programs that will take this raw recording, analyze the wave patterns, and determine the binary data they're encoding.  For 2000 baud, a program called Ballybin can do this.  For 300 baud, there's a program called KCS, and a suite of programs called the Casio Utilities (since they were originally made for Casio computer programs).

Once I've processed the recordings to get this binary data, I can turn it back into a .wav file that will have no noise, so it will load into an Astrocade without errors, and the .wav file will also compress very well.  For 2000 baud programs, a program called Astrowav does this.  KCS can do this for 300 baud programs.  There's also a program called prg2txt that will take a binary 300 baud program and turn it into a .txt file of the source code.  I don't know of a good way to do this for 2000 baud programs.

All the tools I've mentioned can be found here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/tape_archive_tools/tape_archive_tools.html

Is there any part of this process you'd like more information on?

Paul

> When I archive a program from tape, the first thing I do is to play the
> tape into my sound card and record it in an audio editing program,
> Audacity. I then save this as a .wav file. .wav is an uncompressed
> audio file format used, for example, on CDs. Since this hasn't been
> processed in any way to improve the quality, we call this a raw
> recording.
>
> There are programs that will take this raw recording, analyze the wave
> patterns, and determine the binary data they're encoding. For 2000
> baud, a program called Ballybin can do this. For 300 baud, there's a
> program called KCS, and a suite of programs called the Casio Utilities
> (since they were originally made for Casio computer programs).
>
> Once I've processed the recordings to get this binary data, I can turn
> it back into a .wav file that will have no noise, so it will load into
> an Astrocade without errors, and the .wav file will also compress very
> well. For 2000 baud programs, a program called Astrowav does this.
> KCS can do this for 300 baud programs. There's also a program called
> prg2txt that will take a binary 300 baud program and turn it into a
> .txt file of the source code. I don't know of a good way to do this
> for 2000 baud programs.

10164:
Not to be too confusing, but I think you have it backwards,
Bally ans ASTRO BASICs did memory sharing. One byte went to the screen RAM and
the other byte went to the program. Every time you run a program, the screen
byte has to be extracted and the program byte remained, and then had to be acted
upon (deciphered), thus the microcycler. The Bally BASIC did the ectraction each
and every byte of the program. In Astro, however, The program line was extracted
and put in the line input buffer. It was then acted upon from there.
Mike White's UNPACK program extracted the two into 2 separate programs. This is
how the extended BASIC's do the program. This also allows the extended BASIC's
to give you 4 colors and run extremely fast. Take for example my Spring Thing
Part 1 program, or Mike Peace's Outpost 19, or his Gate Escape. These programs
would be considerably slower if they needed to be extracted from the screen
memory.
When the program is UNPACKed, you can take use of the extensive editing
capabilities in BRB1.1. When finished, you can used REPACK to put the screen and
program back together. Record it, and then play it is the original basic. You
can also make a sceen dump for the Bally BASIC this way.
Any questions?
Ken

Paul Thacker wrote:
>>
Line 25 spelled out PRINT instead of using a keyword. Is this really what you want to do?
>>

With so many potential warnings, then it would be just like using Windows Vista!

In case you're not aware, in extended BASICs, you CAN spell out keywords.  You can also use abbreviated keywords.  For instance, in Blue Ram BASIC, you can type any of the following and they are functionally the same:

10 PRINT"A"  (using Shift-Word "PRINT")
10 PR."A"    (Using an abbreviation for "PRINT")
10 PRINT"A"  (typing each letter separately)

You may think that these lines are then tokenized and each form of "PRINT" is stored as 116, but that is NOT the case.  If you edit this line, you'll see that each form of the line has kept the form that was used to type it in.  This means that using Word-Shift "Print" uses one byte while using the typed-out form of P,R,I,N,T uses five bytes and the abbreviated version uses three bytes.  So, if you're counting bytes, then the old-fashioned Word-Shift version is still the best one to use.

To Use "Repack:"

1.  Key in utility and put on permanent storage tape.
2.  Key in program text, variables, strings and machine code in stack area.
3.  Tape all at once!!
    NOTE: You limits are from simple :PRINT, or rather:
          from :PRINT %(16384),1864 to :PRINT %(16384),1987 [half the stack]
4.  Press [Reset] and key in picture program or load AB Scribbling.
    NOTE: Try putting: IF &(23):PRINT into Scribbling somewhere
          and hit left key column to dump [if Scribbling was used].
6.  Load "Repack."
7.  Load Text at "AWAITING INPUT OF TEXT"
8:  Load picture at "READY TO LOAD PICTURE"
9:  Choose File Search. [To follow Vol.5, Pg. 12 Arcadian "File Searcher"]
10.  Dump finished program to tape.

I have now finished typing, playing and debugging the 2000-baud version of "Sink the U-Boat" by L&M Software.  I have not beat the computer "player," but that's okay.  I cheated and set the variable "F" to "1" which means that I DID win.  Then I used GOTO 800 to check if I won... and what do you know-- I did!  So, the game went through the code sequence to show that I won.  After playing a long game and then cheating to show the "player won" sequence, I'm comfortable that there are no errors in the game.

The only trouble that I really had when I was playing to make sure that there were no errors in the game is that the enemy sub was attacking its own side of the screen.  Then, when I would enter my attack coordinates, the game would hang.  Well, it APPEARED to hang.  When I used TRACE, the game kept going over and over to line 130.  Line 130 is:

130 R=RND(30)+30;IF@(B)=1GOTO130

I checked B, and B was 1, which meant that line 130 was in an infinite loop!  As it turns out, line 130 shouldn't read R=RND, is should be B=RND.  I'm not sure if that's my error or not.  The handwriting for the code of the game really DOES LOOK like an R-- but it might be a poorly written B.  Who knows?  Either way, it's SUPPOSED to be a B.  I fixed that and now the game plays just fine.

I used PRINT SZ and the result is 155.  So, the program does use about 1,650 bytes of memory.  Which is pretty-much all of it.

"Sink the U-Boat" isn't really fun because there is absolutely no strategy at all.  Basically, the enemy sub chooses a place to hide from 1-30, then I choose a place from 31-60 to hide.  Then we shoot at each other.  Then we can move to ANY space that hasn't been shot before.  This game is sort of a graphical makeover of an simple Guess-the-Number game.  You know, I'm thinking of a number between 1-30, what is it?.  The difference is that I don't tell you if your guess is hot or cold or high or low.  I've played other similar games that WERE fun and the only difference is that you and the computer could move only ONE square at a time between rounds.  In this game, you just keep guessing blinding until one of you randomly hits the other.  What's the fun in that?

I'm STILL happy that I archived this program because I learned that this game's graphics are EXTREMELY simple.  The subs, which don't look bad at all, are drawn with multiple boxes (a VERY common technique in the early Bally BASIC days).  This was couple of years before Mike Skala wrote a tutorial in the November 1982 issue of the Arcadian about how to use the Display Character (CHRDIS) routine in the System ROM.  The CHRDIS routine was known LONG before this tutorial, but this tutorial, it seems, made the routine more generally known (and understood) so that others could use CHRDIS too.  Soon, all the games used it.  CHRDIS made drawing graphics faster-- PLUS, it used less memory!  What a bonus!

I still need to digitally archive "Sink the U-Boat," as it currently is still in analog form (but store digitally-- hmm, that sounds confusing).  Also, I want to try to add a loading screen to this program if I can figure-out "Repack."  It's VERY likely that this will all wait until tomorrow.

> In case you're not aware, in extended BASICs, you CAN spell out keywords.

> you can type any of the following and they are functionally the same:
>
> 10 PRINT"A"  (using Shift-Word "PRINT")
> 10 PR."A"    (Using an abbreviation for "PRINT")
> 10 PRINT"A"  (typing each letter separately)
>
> You may think that these lines are then tokenized and each form of "PRINT"
> is stored as 116, but that is NOT the case.  If you edit this line, you'll
> see that each form of the line has kept the form that was used to type it
> in.  This means that using Word-Shift "Print" uses one byte while using the
> typed-out form of P,R,I,N,T uses five bytes and the abbreviated version
> uses three bytes.  So, if you're counting bytes, then the old-fashioned
> Word-Shift version is still the best one to use.

I finally used/tested txt2prg, the program that allows you to type text files on your PC and translate them to a binary file which can be translated to a 300-baud WAV file via another Windows command line program called KCS.  I used "Video:Video" by Fred Rodney (another program that Paul requested to be typed in) as the test program.  I'm not sure if "Video:Video" has any errors in it or not, as I couldn't tell the difference between several of the "plus" signs and "division" signs in the program listing in the Arcadian.  "Video:Video" runs and seems to work okay-- at least to the extent that I used it.

Here is the process that I used to take a program typed-in using Windows Notepad and ended up with a 2000-Baud program:

1) Typed the program in Notepad in Windows XP.

2) Used "txt2prg" to create a binary "prg" file.  I had made several errors that "txt2prg" did catch so that they didn't make their way into the final program.  Well... all right!

3) Used KCS on Windows XP to translate the "prg" file to a 300-Baud WAV file.

4) Loaded the 300-Baud WAV file into AstroBASIC (the BASIC with the built-in audio interface) using Jay Fenton's "300-Baud to 2000-Baud Translator" from the AstroBASIC manual.  In the end I didn't want a 300-Baud program-- that's just too slow for me!

5) Saved "Video:Video" from AstroBASIC as a 2000-Baud file.

6) Ran "Video:Video" in AstroBASIC.  Fixed one syntax error (I missed typing a semi-colon).

7) Allowed "Video:Video" to run.  It draws some pretty shapes on the screen-- it seems similar to early Bally BASIC programs that create "Video Art," but this one is a bit more complicated.

I'm not sure how to use "Video:Video," as their are no docs.  There are features that I'm not using, and I can tell just by looking at the code.  For instance, I should be able to save the picture on the screen via :PRINT.  That's not important to me though, I just wanted to test out txt2prg-- I'm happy to report that it was super easy to use.

Thanks for your work on this program, Ronaldo!  For someone that's never owned a Bally/Astrocade, nor even seen one (right?), I think you've done the Bally community a BIG favor by creating this program.  Now that I've used this program once, I'm SURE that I'll use it again!

I know that the above steps to get the "Video:Video" saved as a 2000-Baud program are convoluted... but that's not the fault of Ronaldo and his program.  His program is meant to convert a text file to a binary file for use with KCS-- and it does that job VERY well indeed.

Last night I took a cursory look into the Bob Fabris collection ("a cursory look" still took about forty-five minutes).  I was looking for the original program print-out of "Video:Video."  If I could find that, then I could perhaps use it to tell the difference between the "plus" signs and "division" signs.  I didn't find the original printout, but I did decide to take a look at the source of the Arcadian photocopies that Bob would send out.  I quickly found Arcadian Vol. 11/12, Pg. 113, which has the printout of the program, although even THIS is a copy of the original program (since it has been reduced in size to fit the newsletter).

This means that the Arcadian scans online are really fourth or fifth generation copies for most programs.  Here is how that works:

1)  Generation 1 - Original printout of program, usually made onto thermal silver-color paper.

2)  Generation 2 - Reduced-in-size program printout.  Programs were shrunk-down so that the Arcadian could fit more content.  Often programs were shrunk to about 50% of the original size.  This became more common in the later issues of the Arcadian, perhaps as more content was available, and then in the later years, the programs were sometimes printed full-size.

3)  Generation 3 - Reduced-in-size program copy used in cut and paste version of Arcadian.  This version was referred to as the "master" but as can be seen, this "master" is really already a third-generation copy.

4)  Generation 4 - Photocopied version of Arcadian from "master" version.

5)  Generation 5 - Scanned versions of Arcadian online at BallyAlley.com made from fourth-generation copies.

Sometimes programs were not reduced in size, so step 3 would use a first-generation printout.

After a reduction in size, which makes a program printout harder to read to begin with, and using a 5'th Generation Copy from online, it's no wonder that difficult to read symbols like "divide" and "plus" become "smudged" over time.  Those are not the only problem symbols either, but many others are easy to tell from the syntax used in the BASIC program.

Saying all this, using the third-generation printout for reference, the program "Video:Video" is only slightly easier to read.  The true problem here seems to be that the reduction in size really did a number on some of the symbols.

10210:
That IS the 512-color palette MESS uses - the low bit is used to
switch "Stars" on and off in the MAME emulations of Arcade games.

Since the Astrocade has no starfield, it only uses the Even colors
so WHITE is at 7 times 2 equals 14, a step dimmer than 15 (White).

Instead of Red/Green/Blue values of 255/255/255 this leaves us with
Light Gray at 238/238/238 - which is still brighter than yours is.

Richard

You did some really cool archive work with General Video Assembler!  You've got the know-how, and what REALLY counts when archiving an assembler that requires WORK tapes: patience.  The General Video Assembler came out in the later days of the Astrocade's lifetime and required RAM expansion, so few people ever gave it a whirl.  Most people who dabbled in machine language on the Bally/Astrocade programed by hand.  There is some evidence in the Bob Fabris collection that some people used CP/M cross-assemblers (and of course Brett used a TRS-80 hooked DIRECTLY to the Astrocade), but most ML routines were painfully "assembled" by hand.

This isn't a new version of Brett Bilbrey's "Critter."  However, I DID modify it so that it now runs in AstroBASIC.  I only had to modified two bytes of the machine language source code.  The Bally BASIC code called the Bally BASIC Interrupt Routine.  The AstroBASIC Interrupt Routine is in a different location, so of course "Critter" didn't work in the newer version of BASIC.  We actually knew this, but I can't recall anyone recently ( that is in the past ten years since the start of the Bally Alley discussion group) or in any of the newsletters "fixing" the program for AstroBASIC.  I changed the program so that it makes a CALL to the AstroBASIC Interrupt Routine instead of the Bally BASIC routine.  Now it works without trouble.

I change the Bally BASIC version from this:

130 D=-20275;gosub C
140 D=-3296;gosub C

to this:

130 D=-563;gosub C
140 D=-3295;gosub C

Here is what the change looks like in assembly language (it makes more sense this way):

The Bally BASIC version had this at location $4CE3:

CALL $20B0 ; Call Bally BASIC's Interrupt Routine

It was changed to this:

CALL $21FD ; Call AstroBASIC's Interrupt Routine

The one change required two line changes in the AstroBASIC program.

For those interested, here is "Critter" in BASIC with the changes needed to run the program in AstroBASIC.  This code can be copied and pasted into a file and then run through txt2prg, then through KCS.  This will create a 300-Baud program.  Finally, this program can be loaded as a 300-BAUD file using the "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Converter."  You DON'T need the 300-Baud interface to do any of this.  Here is the program (bring back any memories, Brett?):

For those that REALLY want to know what's going on behind the scenes, he is the assembly listing, you can assemble this with Zmac, if you want.  It won't run though, as the program needs to be entered into BASIC using, you guessed it, the BASIC program (above).  This will let you understand what the heck the BASIC program is doing (that is, if you understand Z80 assembly language and have looked through the "Nutting Manual").


; Critter - For the Bally Astrocade
; File Name: Crit2000.ASM
; Version 1.4 - March 2, 2011 (Modified for AstroBASIC)
; Version 1.3 - February 12, 2002
;
; This source is as it appears in the PEEK N' POKE
; manual.  It has only been changed so that it
; runs under AstroBASIC and assembles under Zmac;
; the Z80 code it generates is EXACTLY the same
; as the BASIC listing.
; When assembled, this will NOT run as a cartridge!
; Critter does not run without the first version of
; Bally BASIC; Critter does NOT run under Astro BASIC
; (it needs vector modifications).
;
; Compile with:
; zmac -i -m -o critterp.bin -x critterp.lst critterp.asm

MCALL   EQU  $06
MRET    EQU  $08
VECT    EQU  $3E

        ORG  $4C80
        DI
        EXX
        LD   A,$4C
        LD   I,A   ;Load I with page of interrupt vector
        LD   A,$E0
        OUT  ($0D),A    ; Load custom chips with line of
        EXX             ; interrupt vector
        EI
        RET

        ORG  $4CE0
        DW   $4CE3      ; Points to interrupt routine
       
        ORG  $4CE3
;       CALL $20B0      ; Call Bally BASIC interrupt routine
        CALL $21FD      ; Call AstroBASIC interrupt routine
        DI
        LD   ($4C70),SP ; Save SP
        LD   SP,$4C70   ; Move SP
        PUSH AF
        PUSH BC
        PUSH DE
        PUSH HL
        PUSH IX
        PUSH IY
        IN   A,($1C)    ; Get KN(1) value
        LD   ($4D3A),A  ; Place in vector block
        RST  $38        ; On-board call
        DB   $00        ;Routine 01 - Start Multiple Calls
        DB   MCALL+1    ; Call V Write Routine
        DW   VWRITE
        DB   VECT+1     ; Move vector (see ROM manual)
        DW   VBLOCK     ; Vector Block Address
        DW   LIMITS     ; Limit Table
        DB   MCALL+1    ; Call V Write Routine
        DW   VWRITE
        DB   $02        ; Routine 02 - End Multiple Calls
        POP  IY
        POP  IX
        POP  HL
        POP  DE
        POP  BC
        POP  AF
        LD   SP,($4C70) ; Return SP
        EI
        RET

        ORG  $4D18
VWRITE: DB   $1F        ; Routine 30 - VWRITR
        DW   $4D38      ; Vector
        DW   $4D24      ; Pattern
        DB   MRET

        ORG  $4D20
; Limit Table

LIMITS: DB   00D,152D      ; X boundaries
        DB   00D,64D       ; Y boundaries
        DB   00D,00D       ; (0,0) Position
        DB   $02,$08       ; 2 byte, 8 line pattern size

; Critter pattern
        DW   $A00A     
        DW   $8822
        DW   $AAAA
        DW   $A82A
        DW   $2008
        DW   $0820
        DW   $2008
        DW   $0000

; VECTOR BLOCK (See 'Nutting' ROM Manual, page 39-41)
VBLOCK: DB     $20     ; Magic Register value
        DB     $80     ; Vector Status
        DB     $00     ; Time Base - Holds KN(1) value
        DW     $0005   ; Delta X
        DW     $0000   ; X Position
        DB     $03     ; X Checks Mask -Bounce off walls
        DW     $0005   ; Delta Y
        DW     $0000   ; Y Position
        DB     $03     ; Y Checks Mask -Bounce off walls


I'm sure that being posted to the discussion group probably has really done wonders to the spacing of both the BASIC program and the assembly language listing.  For those that wonder if the BASIC program and the output of the source code match byte-for-byte with the machine language input via BASIC, they both match exactly (I double-checked this morning).

If anyone's eyes are boggling... don't worry.  This is actually a very short program.  Despite what it looks like above, the program is only 114 bytes.  Since I'm in a REALLY geeky mood today, here is the program in machine code in 60-column format (as it just STRETCHED if I didn't put carriage-returns):

F3D93E4CED473EE0D30DD9FBC9E34C00CDFD21F3ED73704C31704CF5C5D5
E5DDE5FDE5DB1C323A4DFF0007184D3F384D204D07184D02FDE1DDE1E1D1
C1F1ED7B704CFBC9001F384D244D08000000980040000002080AA02288AA
AA2AA8082020080820000020800005000000030500000003

It is the responsibility of the BASIC program to take these hexadecimal numbers, that are input in decimal form, and put them in memory where they are SUPPOSED to go, as these number can NOT be stringed all together starting at one location in memory.

2) Take a binary file (for instance, output from an assembler), and load it at any location desired.  This would allow for creating short ML routines on the Astrocade without the need to type in long @() arrays or the method that "Critter" uses, which is pretty tedious (but was a tiny baby step in the right direction in 1980!).

10242:
Brett Bilbrey wrote:
>>
In my defense, [the "Critter" ML ;oader] was only the first means I came up with to load machine code.  Later I developed a more compact loader that worked on strings (like others did).
>>

It is worth noting that there were quite a few ways to get machine language into Bally BASIC.  Brett's method in "Critter" is very straight forward and gets the job done.  It also happens to be among the first ML loaders printed in any newsletter (if not THE first loader).  There were a few printed programs that allowed a user to input bytes a few at a time, but nothing that was a routine written in ML.  Later the newsletters had a sprinkling of programs with some ML code, but there was never a floodgate that opened and suddenly users were writing lots of machine language programs.  This was really the case with most microcomputers: ML was time consuming to program in and most home computer programmers were only dabbling their feet in the programming waters.  That why back then BASIC was king.

Adam

I can already see that Richard has answered your posting.  Fast!

This is a good opportunity to add that typing in programs for ANY computer has always been prone to trouble.  It requires quite a bit of patience, but even more than patience, it requires very careful proofreading.  Think about it.  The Astrocade only has 1,800 bytes that can be used for a BASIC program.  Some programs that fill EVERY single byte have the user also fill in arrays with direct commands.  That is nearly 2,000 chances to make an error.  I've always thought that even a type-in program that seems to run perfectly may very well have an error in it.

What about more popular computers like the Commodore 64 that had about 40K of usable BASIC programming area?  Those BASIC programs could be real monsters to type in.  I used to pick up "Compute's Gazette" magazine back in the day for $2.95.  I would actually type some of those beasts in... when for $12.95 there was a version of the magazine that included a disk with all those programs included.  I was a teenager and I didn't have thirteen bucks-- but I did have three bucks to spend.

I wouldn't be surprised at all to learn that some of the archived programs on BallyAlley.com have some typos in them, either from the typist, or as Paul and I have been recently discovering, from mistakes in the original program listing that went unreported... at least to us.  Even a perfectly archived tape without any archiving errors may have problems like this.

I always imagined when I was a teenager that there were MANY people typing in these programs on the Commodore 64, but I was surprised to learn a few years ago that even at the very height of the publication of "Compute's Gazette" only about 90,000 copies were printed a month.  Of those readers, how many people actually took the time to type the programs in?  What about on other computer platforms?

Even if you were not a programmer, did YOU type programs in from BASIC listings?

Adam
